name: Xanthomonas bacterial leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-dependent bacterial leaf-spot diagnosis. Historical hemp evidence describes small water-soaked lesions that develop approximately 1–2 mm necrotic centers with comparatively broad 2–3 mm yellow halos, but fungal disease, other bacteria, arthropods, exposure injury, edema, and Cannabis salt-excretion injury can overlap visually.
affectedParts: stems and young shoots for exclusion of nutrient-salt deposits and other syndromes
stages: growth stage not established in Cannabis-specific Xanthomonas evidence
vegetative or reproductive stage must be recorded rather than inferred from lesion appearance
indicators: Small water-soaked spots are visible in intact leaf tissue before the centers become necrotic.
The water-soaked area transitions to a discrete brown or dark necrotic center rather than remaining a superficial removable deposit.
Necrotic centers in the Japanese hemp report were approximately 1–2 mm in diameter.
Yellow halos in that report were approximately 2–3 mm wide.
The chlorotic halo is proportionally wider than the necrotic center in the documented Cannabis lesion geometry.
Comparable focal lesions occur on more than one attached leaf and can be mapped on both leaf surfaces rather than appearing only as one detached spot.
Serial views preserve the water-soaked-to-necrotic-with-halo sequence instead of a stable crystal, residue, glare, or camera-color artifact.
A high-confidence causal label requires a representative active lesion linked to bacterial recovery and validated molecular or genomic identification consistent with Xanthomonas cannabis.

The UF/IFAS institutional composite shows that compatible presentation can combine broader whole-plant yellowing or blighting with multiple discrete necrotic, yellow-haloed spots on individual leaflets.

Figure 15 combines whole-plant and close lesion views but supplies no visible scale, plant or sample identifier, laboratory result, isolate, sequence accession, or current species-level linkage for the pictured material.
exclusions: White surface colonies, fungal fruiting structures, diagnostic conidia, or a positive fungal assay support powdery mildew or a fungal leaf spot rather than Xanthomonas.
Fine stippling, silver scarring, webbing, fecal spots, eggs, mites, thrips, or other organisms on the leaf underside support arthropod feeding.
Damage follows spray droplets, rubbing points, a documented chemical application, heat, or high light and does not progress after that exposure ends.
Symptoms follow a measured older-leaf or younger-leaf nutrient-mobility pattern without discrete water-soaked lesions and broad halos.
White crystalline patches cluster around non-glandular trichomes or along veins and stems, excess nutrient salts are documented, and culture, sequencing, or fungal PCR does not support a pathogen.
Dark angular or vein-limited lesions, red bacterial streaming, or laboratory evidence supports Serratia marcescens or another bacterial disease.
A plant diagnostic laboratory identifies another pathogen or abiotic cause from a representative active lesion, or Xanthomonas is recovered only as an unlinked epiphyte or contaminant.
A genome, species name, virulence marker, culture image, or non-Cannabis isolate is available without the photographed Cannabis lesion and plant linkage needed for causal attribution.

progression.description: A small water-soaked area appears within an attached leaf blade. Capture both surfaces, scale, node, leaf age, and the surrounding healthy tissue before necrosis obscures this early feature.
The central tissue darkens and becomes necrotic while the spot remains small and discrete; the Japanese hemp report described centers approximately 1–2 mm across.
A yellow border develops around the necrotic center and was approximately 2–3 mm wide in the historical report, producing a halo wider than the center.

Map whether compatible lesions appear on additional attached leaves and whether old lesions change while new water-soaked lesions emerge. Cannabis evidence does not establish a universal canopy, leaf-age, coalescence, defoliation, stem, or flower sequence.

Link the imaged active lesion to culture and validated molecular or genomic evidence. If testing supports another organism, salt-excretion injury, or no causal plant-linked Xanthomonas, retain the visual sequence only as an unresolved look-alike.

lookAlikes: Excess-nutrient salt excretion from non-glandular trichomes
Nutrient deficiency, toxicity, or unsuitable root-zone pH
confirmation: Do not confirm Xanthomonas cannabis from water-soaking, a yellow halo, lesion dimensions, bacterial streaming, one photograph, or one video; cap image/video-only confidence at 0.20.

Capture serial whole-plant and upper-, middle-, and lower-canopy views plus both surfaces of multiple attached leaves under neutral repeatable lighting, with scale, color reference, node and leaf age, and a healthy same-cultivar comparison.

Record cultivar, propagation source, stage, onset date, lesion counts and positions, irrigation and splash events, humidity or leaf-wetness context, fertilizer and spray history, pH, EC, and whether surface material wipes or dissolves away.
Submit fresh, recently expanding lesions containing the healthy-to-affected margin to a plant diagnostic laboratory; keep samples separate, cool, and dry according to that laboratory’s instructions.

Ask the laboratory to distinguish bacterial, fungal, arthropod, and abiotic injury using microscopy, culture, and appropriate assays; bacterial streaming supports suspicion but can be absent and is not species confirmation.

If Xanthomonas is recovered, require validated molecular or genomic identification and plant linkage; report isolate, method, sequence or accession where available, current Xanthomonas cannabis taxonomy, historical synonym, and any justified pathovar without inferring host causality from species identity alone.

Admit an image or video as confirmed reference data only when the exact plant and lesion are linked to adequate diagnostic evidence, rights, attribution, source grouping, and human review; otherwise retain it as suspected, unresolved, or metadata-only.
immediateActions: Flag the plant and pause movement of cuttings or symptomatic foliage until laboratory triage.
Handle suspect foliage only when dry, avoid splash between plants, and clean hands and tools before moving to unaffected plants.
Keep unconfirmed lesion photographs out of bacterial ground-truth and training sets.
correctivePlan: Base removal, sanitation, and any crop treatment on the confirmed diagnosis and local legal label; a visual bacterial-leaf-spot suspicion is not a treatment prescription.
Inspect nearby plants for comparable small haloed lesions and document whether new lesions appear after splash or handling events without treating that association as proof.
If laboratory results do not recover or identify the bacterium, reopen fungal, arthropod, chemical, and physiological differentials.
prevention: Use documented healthy propagation material and retain lot or mother-plant traceability.
Minimize leaf wetness and splash during routine handling where compatible with the production system.
Disinfect tools and segregate symptomatic material under a written sanitation protocol.
warnings: A photograph or video cannot confirm Xanthomonas cannabis; lesion size and halo geometry are triage features only.

The key symptom measurements come from a historical Japanese hemp report and do not establish current local prevalence, cultivar susceptibility, production-system risk, or a universal late-stage sequence.
Xanthomonas cannabis is genetically and host diverse; a species-level result, virulence marker, or non-Cannabis pathogenicity assay is not by itself proof of causal Cannabis disease.

Cannabis excess-nutrient salt injury can produce pathogen-like leaf spots, necrosis, blighting, wilt, and white deposits; surface appearance must remain linked to exposure, microscopy, and pathogen exclusions.
General greenhouse bacterial-leaf-spot guidance is used only for differential diagnosis and handling precautions, not as Cannabis-specific epidemiological proof.

UF/IFAS Figure 15 is an attributed institutional composite, not a plant- and lesion-linked laboratory record; its CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license prohibits derivatives and commercial reuse without permission.
The reference lacks scale, sample identity, culture, microscopy, sequence accessions, pathogenicity linkage, and a current Xanthomonas cannabis identification for the pictured plant.
No plant-linked, laboratory-confirmed Cannabis image or video with verified item-level automated-training permission was found; the new reference remains metadata-only and training-ineligible.

sources.title: Bacterial leaf spot of hemp caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Japan
sources.publisher: Springer Nature on behalf of the Phytopathological Society of Japan
supportedClaims: The cannabis-specific Japanese report described leaf lesions with necrotic centers approximately 1–2 mm in diameter and yellow halos approximately 2–3 mm wide.
Pathological, physiological, and genetic characterization linked the Japanese causal bacterium to the organism historically named Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis in Romania.

sources.title: Comparative genomics of a cannabis pathogen reveals insight into the evolution of pathogenicity in Xanthomonas
supportedClaims: Cannabis bacterial leaf spot was described as water-soaked lesions followed by necrosis with a yellow halo.
The study sequenced two geographically distinct strains previously isolated from symptomatic cannabis tissue in Japan and Romania and proposed the species name Xanthomonas cannabis.

sources.title: Field Guide to Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Diseases
sources.publisher: University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension
supportedClaims: The UF/IFAS field guide describes Xanthomonas-associated hemp injury as small necrotic leaf spots with yellow or chlorotic halos, leaf yellowing, and blighting.
UF/IFAS Figure 15 is a four-panel institutional hemp reference credited to Rui Yang, Joshua Freeman, and Mathews Paret; it combines a whole potted-plant view with multiple leaf and lesion close-ups.

The guide states that bacteria can enter through natural openings or wounds and that excessive moisture or extended leaf wetness can increase disease intensity, while emphasizing that little is known about this hemp disease complex.

The guide recommends plant-diagnostic-center pathogen identification and confirmation; Figure 15 is therefore a visual differential rather than specimen-linked laboratory or current species-level proof.
The publication is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, limiting reuse to unchanged noncommercial distribution with attribution and excluding derivative preparation without additional permission.

sources.title: Species: Xanthomonas cannabis
sources.organization: List of Prokaryotic names with Standing in Nomenclature (LPSN)
supportedClaims: Xanthomonas cannabis (ex Severin 1978) McKnight et al. 2026 is the validly published correct species name.
The historical names Xanthomonas campestris pv. cannabis and the 2015 proposed name “Xanthomonas cannabis” are homotypic synonyms; type strain identifiers include ICMP 6570, LMG 9042, and NCPPB 2877.

sources.title: Comparative genomics of ‘Xanthomonas cannabis’ reveals an emerging, diverse pathogen
supportedClaims: Whole-genome comparison placed historically collected isolates from Zinnia and Cucurbita within the genetically diverse Xanthomonas cannabis species even though those isolates were not recovered from Cannabis.

The Australian isolates differed in phylogroup and virulence-associated gene content, and their pathogenic potential was assessed on seven non-Cannabis hosts; species identity or virulence-gene content alone therefore does not prove that an arbitrary isolate caused a Cannabis lesion.

The study compiled Cannabis-, Abelmoschus-, Phaseolus-, Solanum-, and Zinnia-associated members and four proposed pathovars, supporting isolate-, pathovar-, host-, and plant-linkage reporting rather than treating the species name as a visually uniform disease label.

sources.title: Non-glandular trichomes (epidermal hairs) in cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) plants are capable of excreting nutrient salts under excessive fertilizer regimes
supportedClaims: Hydroponic Cannabis plants developed leaf spots, foliar necrosis and blighting, wilt, and superficial white stem patches that visually resembled pathogen injury.

Culture, whole-genome sequencing, and fungal-specific PCR did not identify a causal fungal or bacterial pathogen; light and scanning electron microscopy plus X-ray microanalysis instead linked white crystalline deposits to salts extruded from non-glandular trichomes.

Excess nutrient-salt treatments reproduced compatible injury, making measured nutrient exposure, crystalline surface deposits, microscopy, and pathogen testing important exclusions before a bacterial-leaf-spot label.
The observations involved one named production genotype and controlled excess-salt treatments, so their timing, appearance, and severity are not universal Cannabis thresholds.

sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Spot on Greenhouse Ornamentals
supportedClaims: Across greenhouse ornamental hosts, bacterial and fungal leaf spots can be visually confounded; bacterial streaming can support suspicion but may be absent, and diagnosis by a plant disease clinic is recommended.

As general bacterial-leaf-spot precautions rather than cannabis-specific epidemiology, splashing water and handling wet plants can spread bacteria, so suspect plants should be handled dry and separately.
